title: Chef Kunal Kapur's Dhaniya Wale Aloo: A Simple Monsoon Comfort Recipe
excerpt: The celebrity chef shares his take on the classic coriander-spiced potato dish, a North Indian staple perfect for rainy-day meals
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Chef Kunal Kapur's dhaniya wale aloo is a quick, flavourful potato dish coated in coriander chutney.
  • The recipe requires minimal ingredients and takes about 40 minutes to prepare.
  • It's naturally vegan, gluten-free, and suitable for Navratri fasting with rock salt.
  • The dish pairs well with phulkas, parathas, or can be enjoyed as a standalone snack.

  • Chef Kunal Kapur's dhaniya wale aloo is a quick, flavourful potato dish coated in fresh coriander chutney
  • The recipe requires minimal ingredients — boiled potatoes, a fresh coriander paste, and basic spices — with about 40 minutes of total cooking time
  • The dish is naturally vegan (when made with oil instead of ghee), gluten-free, and suitable for Navratri fasting with rock salt
  • It pairs well with phulkas, parathas, or as a standalone snack during the monsoon season

As monsoon rains sweep across India, few dishes capture the season's comfort-food spirit quite like dhaniya wale aloo — boiled potatoes tossed in a bright, herbaceous coriander chutney. Celebrity chef Kunal Kapur recently shared his version of this North Indian classic on his YouTube channel, describing it as "hatke, super easy and packed with flavour in every bite."

Kapur, known for his accessible approach to traditional Indian cooking, presented the dish as an everyday meal that delivers bold taste with minimal effort — the kind of recipe that "you'll want on your menu again and again."

The Recipe

Dhaniya wale aloo starts with baby potatoes, boiled in a pressure cooker until cooked but still firm. The star of the dish is the dhaniya (coriander) chutney: a cup of roughly chopped fresh coriander leaves blended with green chilli, an inch of ginger, and a splash of water into a smooth, vibrant paste.

The cooking is straightforward. Heat ghee (or oil for a vegan version) in a heavy-bottomed pan on low flame. Add cumin powder, black pepper, garam masala, and rock salt. Toss in the boiled potatoes and sauté until lightly roasted — about 10 minutes. Then fold in the coriander chutney, coating each potato, and let everything simmer for another 10 minutes until the flavours meld.

A squeeze of lemon juice at the end brightens the dish, and a garnish of dry-roasted sesame seeds adds crunch.

Ingredients at a Glance

The full ingredient list is simple: 500 grams baby potatoes, one cup coriander leaves, one green chilli, one inch ginger, half a teaspoon each of cumin powder, black pepper, and garam masala, two teaspoons lemon juice, two teaspoons roasted sesame seeds, one tablespoon ghee, and rock salt to taste. Total prep and cooking time runs about 40 minutes, serving four.

Why It Works for Monsoon

The dish ticks several boxes that make it ideal for India's rainy season. It is warm and mildly spiced without being heavy. Fresh coriander, which is abundant and affordable during the monsoon, provides both flavour and a nutritional boost — the herb is rich in vitamins A, C, and K. The rock salt variant makes it suitable for Navratri fasting, when onion and garlic are avoided.

"Fresh coriander, bold masalas and comforting desi vibes… total winner for everyday meals!" — Chef Kunal Kapur

Chef Kunal Kapur's Approach

Kapur, a Michelin-trained chef who has become one of India's most-followed culinary personalities on social media, built his reputation on making traditional recipes approachable. His YouTube channel features hundreds of recipes spanning regional Indian cuisines, with an emphasis on home cooking techniques that don't require professional equipment.

His dhaniya wale aloo fits this philosophy — it requires no specialty ingredients, no advanced technique, and comes together in under an hour. The recipe is also highly adaptable; some home cooks add roasted peanuts for extra protein, or substitute the chutney with a mint-coriander blend for a different flavour profile.

A Diaspora Kitchen Staple

For the Indian diaspora, dhaniya wale aloo occupies a particular niche in the comfort-food rotation. It requires ingredients available at any Indian grocery store — or, increasingly, mainstream supermarkets in cities with significant South Asian populations. The dish evokes monsoon memories for those who grew up eating it with steaming phulkas during July and August rains, and its simplicity makes it a go-to recipe for weeknight dinners abroad.

It also translates well as a side dish at potlucks and gatherings, where its bold green colour and aromatic coriander make it a conversation starter alongside more familiar curries.

What's Next

Kapur continues to roll out seasonal recipes on his channel, and monsoon-specific dishes — pakoras, chai-time snacks, and one-pot meals — have become a regular feature during July and August. For those looking to expand their monsoon menu, dhaniya wale aloo is a quick entry point into the season's flavours, requiring nothing more than a bag of potatoes and a bunch of fresh coriander.
